content: A waveform refers to the specific shape and structure of a signal, such as a wave propagating through a solid, liquid, or gaseous medium. In many instances, the medium through which the wave travels does not allow for a direct visual representation of the wave's form. In such cases, the term waveform is used to describe the shape of a graph that represents the variation of a quantity over time or distance. An oscilloscope is an instrument that can visually display the waveform as a repeating image on a screen, such as a cathode-ray tube (CRT) or liquid crystal display (LCD). Over time, the term waveform has also been extended to describe the graphical representation of any varying quantity as a function of time. Examples of Waveforms 1. Sine Wave: The sine wave is mathematically expressed as sin(2πt). Its amplitude follows a trigonometric sine function with respect to time. This waveform is smooth and periodic, making it fundamental in many physical and engineering applications. 2. Sawtooth Wave: The sawtooth wave is represented by the formula 2(t − floor(t)) − 1. Its shape resembles the teeth of a saw. This waveform is commonly used in time bases for display scanning. It serves as a starting point for subtractive synthesis because a sawtooth wave with a constant period contains both odd and even harmonics, which decrease in amplitude at a rate of −6 dB per octave. 3. Square Wave: The square wave is mathematically described as saw(x) − saw(x − duty). It is widely used to represent digital information. A square wave with a constant period contains only odd harmonics, which also decrease in amplitude at a rate of −6 dB per octave. 4. Triangle Wave: The triangle wave is expressed as (t − 2 floor((t + 1)/2)) (−1)^floor((t + 1)/2). This waveform is the integral of a square wave. It contains only odd harmonics, but their amplitudes decrease more rapidly, at a rate of −12 dB per octave. Other waveforms, often referred to as composite waveforms, can be described as combinations of multiple sinusoidal waves or other basis functions added together. The Fourier series provides a mathematical framework for decomposing periodic waveforms into their fundamental and harmonic components. This means that any periodic waveform can be constructed by summing a fundamental frequency and its harmonics. For non-periodic waveforms with finite energy, the Fourier transform can be used to analyze and decompose them into sinusoidal components. This allows for a detailed understanding of the frequency content of such waveforms.
